svg.text: Entropy: the number of ways, and free energy: the test of spontaneity

g.text: open the partition: each molecule can be in A or B,
so 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3 = 8 arrangements; 5 molecules 2^5 = 32;
100 molecules 2^100; in general x^y for y particles in x places
diffusion happens because there are so many more ways of
spreading out than of staying together; entropy S measures
the number of ways of arranging particles and their energy

svg.text: Comparing standard entropies (J per K per mol)

g.text: state: ice 48.0 < water 69.9 < vapour 188.7
particles: CaO 39.7 < CaCO3 92.9 (more particles, more ways)
hardness: diamond < graphite (stronger forces limit vibration)
reactions: solid to gas, or more moles of gas, means delta S positive
CaCO3(s) to CaO(s) + CO2(g); 2 N2O5(g) to 4 NO2(g) + O2(g): 2 to 5 moles
delta S system = sum S products - sum S reactants
2 Ca + O2 to 2 CaO: 2 x 39.7 - (2 x 41.4 + 205.0) = -208.4 J per K per mol
negative, yet calcium burns: the surroundings' entropy must be counted too

svg.text: delta G = delta H - T delta S

g.text: G is the part of the enthalpy free to do work; TS is the part
tied up in keeping the system at temperature T
delta G negative: spontaneous as written
delta G positive: not spontaneous; the reverse may occur
delta G zero: equilibrium, neither direction spontaneous

svg.text: Sample 6.13: the Haber process at 25 degrees C

g.text: delta G = -91.8 - 298 x (-0.197) = -33.1 kJ: spontaneous
Sample 6.12, CaSO4 dissolving: delta H -17.8 kJ, delta S -0.1447 kJ per K,
delta G = -17.8 + 43.1 = +25.3 kJ: not spontaneous at 25 degrees C

svg.text: Sign of delta G from delta H and delta S

g.text: delta H -, delta S +: always spontaneous
delta H +, delta S -: never spontaneous
delta H -, delta S -: spontaneous at low T (Haber, CaO formation)
delta H +, delta S +: spontaneous at high T (CaCO3 decomposing)

svg.text: Values as printed in topics 6.11 and 6.12. A positive total entropy change (system plus surroundings) is the full test; delta G packages it at constant T and P.
